item.title: Research Paradigms, Methodological Choice, and Historicity in Accounting History
item.content:encoded:
Alan Sangster, University of Aberdeen

Martin Quinn,

Martin Persson,

This special issue examines what drives researchers to select specific historical methods and methodologies when studying accounting history. It seeks to encourage critical examination of how accounting history is conducted, interpreted, and communicated, with emphasis on how research paradigms influence methodological decisions and shape scholarly understanding and debates within the field.

The issue investigates connections between researcher assumptions, source interpretation, and the broader consequences of methodological choices for research quality and credibility. It addresses concerns that insufficient consideration of historicity, evidence quality, contextual factors, and source evaluation practices may lead to misconceptions and controversies in accounting history literature.

The special issue welcomes diverse contributions including empirical, methodological, historiographical, conceptual, and critical papers that substantively engage with improving the methodological rigor, reflexivity, and historical validity of accounting history scholarship. A related workshop will provide opportunities for authors to discuss and develop ideas connected to the special issue's themes.

Potential topics

  • Ontological, epistemological, and axiological positioning in accounting history research
  • Historical method in accounting history research
  • Methodologies in accounting history and their implications for knowledge production
  • Interpretation, validation, and corroboration of primary sources
  • Appropriate and inappropriate uses of secondary sources
  • Source criticism, transparency, and evidential sufficiency in historical research
  • The role of context in the analysis of accounting's past
  • Methodological choices and myths, anomalies, controversies in literature
  • Tensions between theory-driven research and historically grounded inquiry
  • Historical cases as ends versus means to theoretical development
